metadata.title: GraphRAG-ASCOC: A lightweight framework for adaptive synonym-aware clustering and ontology completion
metadata.abstract_summary: This paper presents GraphRAG-ASCOC, a framework for adaptive synonym-aware clustering and ontology completion, which addresses the limitations of text-centric large language model pipelines in converting industrial standards into executable Web Ontology Language ontologies. The framework consists of a synonym-merging module, a multi-feature fusion clustering method, and a lightweight module for recovering implicit relations, and is designed to output compact knowledge bases suitable for intelligent decision support.

sections.heading: Liu
sections.text: a , b , 1 , ∗ a School of Computer and Information Science, Southwest University, Chongqing, 400715, China b Afeka Academic College of Engineering, Tel-Aviv, 610101, Israel a r t i c l e i n f o Keywords: Model-based systems engineering (MBSE) Expert systems Ontology completion GraphRAG-ASCOC Large language models (LLMs) a b s t r a c t Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) are accelerating the shift from document-centric workflows toward the model-driven paradigm of Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE). However, when vast, highly structured industrial standards must be converted into executable Web Ontology Language (OWL) ontologies for expert-system reasoning and decision support, text-centric LLM pipelines suffer from hallucination and context- window limits. Our earlier GraphRAG-KM framework partially mitigated these issues; yet, synonym redundancy, cluster imbalance, and missing relations still constrain downstream reasoning. To address these gaps, we present GraphRAG-ASCOC (Adaptive Synonym-aware Clustering and Ontology Completion), an enhanced, cost-effective, closed-loop pipeline that outputs compact knowledge bases suitable for intelligent decision support. First, a synonym-merging module combines a mutual-nearest-neighbour criterion with FAISS retrieval to consolidate lexi- cal variants and eliminate redundancy. Second, a multi-feature fusion clustering method with a scoring function automatically selects the optimal cluster count, ensuring semantic coherence. Finally, to recover implicit rela- tions, we introduce TLC (TransE–LLM Completion). This lightweight module enriches the ontology with high- confidence triples via embedding recall and semantic validation. To evaluate practical utility, the framework was applied to the U.S. tactical data-link standard MIL-STD-6016B . Experiments demonstrate substantial gains over the original GraphRAG-KM pipeline in entity compression, clustering coherence, and relation-completion F1, producing compact OWL ontologies suitable for rule engines, simulators, and other expert system components. These results confirm the enhanced pipeline’s practical readiness for large-scale defence standards and other in- dustrial documents, paving the way for reliable knowledge bases in real-world expert-system applications across defence and manufacturing domains. 1.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Expert systems and other knowledge-based applications rely on ex- plicit, machine-executable domain models to deliver consistent and ex- plainable decision support ( Otero-Cerdeira et al. , 2015 ). Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) extends this principle by integrating re- quirements, design, verification, and maintenance into coherent models, enabling cross-disciplinary collaboration, traceability, and automated validation throughout the lifecycle ( Estefan , 2007 ). MBSE is now the de facto approach for managing complexity in military communications, aerospace, and advanced manufacturing ( Souri et al. , 2019 ; Wang et al. , 2020 ). ∗ Corresponding author. E-mail address: liubocq@swu.edu.cn (B. Liu). 1 These authors contributed equally to this work. A persistent obstacle is the sheer size and intricacy of the governing technical standards. MIL-STD-6016B, for example, exceeds 6000 pages of protocol definitions, packet formats, and message flows; manual inter- pretation is slow, costly, and prone to inconsistent readings ( U. S. De- partment of Defense , 2024 ). Contemporary MBSE toolchains alleviate this burden by parsing document sections, extracting entities and rela- tions, and mapping them to UML or OWL constructs ( Chen et al. , 2009 ). This enables model-driven simulation, digital twin analysis, and consis- tency checking in large-scale engineering projects ( Gaševic et al. , 2009 ; Singh et al. , 2021 ). In the context of knowledge representation, ontology is a formal specification of a set of concepts and the relationships among them. The TBox defines the classes (con- cepts) and the relationships (properties) between them, while the ABox contains assertions or instances that describe specific knowledge within these classes and properties. These two components are essential for cre- ating semantically rich, logically consistent, and machine-interpretable models ( Cyganiak et al. , 2014 ; Hitzler et al. , 2012 ). Automated pipelines powered by large language models (LLMs) re- duce the manual effort of parsing technical standards by retrieving rel- evant fragments and generating RDF triples (subject–predicate–object) or OWL axioms ( Edge et al. , 2024 ; Wang et al. , 2024 ). Recent studies in Expert Systems with Applications (ESWA) on knowledge graph com- pletion, such as GS-InGAT ( Yin et al. , 2023 ) and GLSEC ( Ma et al. , 2024 ), advance triple prediction on graphs but generally do not address the OWL class axioms required for expert-system reasoning. While MBSE focuses on creating integrated, executable models to manage system complexity, ontology construction ensures those models are semantically rich, logically consistent, and machine-interpretable. Combining MBSE with ontology-driven engineering formalises the knowledge structures needed for model-based validation and reasoning, improving automation, traceability, and logical coherence when repre- senting technical standards. This paper leverages ontology completion to enhance the clarity and consistency of such models in large-scale en- gineering projects. Our previous GraphRAG-KM framework partially bridged this gap by integrating MinerU preprocessing, GraphRAG retrieval, and 𝐾 - Means clustering to generate UML and OWL models from unstruc- tured documents ( Kumar et al. , 2020 ; Wang et al. , 2026 ). sections.heading: Related
sections.text: work Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) has emerged as a domi- nant approach for designing and managing complex systems in domains such as defence communications, aerospace, and advanced manufactur- ing ( Estefan , 2007 ). By formalising system requirements, design, ver- ification, and maintenance into integrated models, MBSE ensures con- sistency and traceability across the system lifecycle. Standardised in- dustrial documents often contain extensive specifications of interfaces and constraints; transforming them into OWL ontologies would enable semantic integration of heterogeneous standards and provide machine- interpretable artefacts for downstream logical verification. However, existing approaches still heavily rely on manual annotation and script- ing, which are labour-intensive, error-prone, and difficult to scale across large technical standard corpora, highlighting the need for more auto- mated solutions ( Arora et al. , 2016 ; Rajbabu et al. , 2018 ). To address this challenge, Lu et al. proposed the GOPPRRE ontol- ogy to support MBSE-driven formalisation and semantic requirement tracing. While their framework constructs domain ontologies based on industrial documentation, it still depends on expert review and lacks an end-to-end pipeline from raw documents to executable ontologies. In scenarios with frequent cross-references and implicit constraints, the extraction performance remains insufficient in efficiency and accuracy, making it unsuitable for rapid industrial iteration ( Lu et al. , 2021 ). In our previous work, we introduced the GraphRAG-KM framework, which combines Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) with industrial knowledge modelling. It represents the first attempt to establish a seamless pipeline from unstructured documents to OWL on- tologies via intermediate knowledge graphs, offering a foundation for rapidly generating MBSE semantic assets. Nevertheless, GraphRAG was initially designed for open-domain question answering and exhibits lim- itations in entity extraction, including its inability to normalise case, plural forms, or semantically similar terms. Its clustering process relies solely on title vectors, and logical reasoning capabilities are restricted, leading to synonym redundancy, imbalanced clusters, and missing rela- tions. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes fine-grained improvements focusing on synonym unification, adaptive clustering, and ontology completion. 2.1. Synonym resolution Facebook AI Similarity Search (FAISS) is a high-performance library designed for efficient approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search in large-scale vector spaces ( Johnson et al. , 2021 ). By leveraging GPU ac- celeration and advanced index structures such as Inverted File (IVF) and Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW), FAISS can perform billion- scale similarity searches over high-dimensional dense vectors within milliseconds. The library has been widely adopted in industry for tasks such as deduplication, recommendation, and large-scale vector similar- ity search ( Johnson et al. , 2017 ; Zilliz Inc. , 2023 ). However, FAISS is typically used in general-purpose settings and re- mains underexplored in ontology engineering, where logical consistency and structured knowledge constraints are critical. This motivates its in- tegration into ontology-driven pipelines for scalable synonym resolu- tion. Mutual Nearest Neighbors (MNN) is an effective strategy for refining candidate matches in embedding space. It selects only those entity pairs that appear in each other’s top-k nearest neighbours, reducing asymmet- ric or noisy alignments ( Haghverdi et al. , 2018 ). MNN has been widely applied in biological data integration, such as aligning single-cell RNA- seq batches, and in semantic matching tasks like paraphrase detection. sections.heading: Methodology
sections.text: Based on the existing GraphRAG-ASCOC pipeline, this work in- troduces targeted improvements along three main threads–dynamic synonym merging, adaptive clustering, and lightweight knowledge completion–forming a closed-loop process of “Merging → Clustering → Completion”. The improved pipeline explicitly eliminates semantic re- dundancies caused by variations in case, plurality, and near-synonym expressions; enhances the consistency of entity clusters through adap- tive cluster sizing and multimodal feature concatenation; and achieves low-cost ontology augmentation via dual-stage filtering using embed- ding retrieval and large language models. Specifically, industrial standard documents often contain multiple expressions for the same concept, such as synonyms, abbreviations, or case variants, leading to entity proliferation. Therefore, we employ vec- tor search and parallel FAISS indexing in the dynamic synonym merg- ing module to group mutually nearest expressions into synonym clus- ters. A decreasing-threshold strategy is further applied to compress the cluster size while respecting a predefined upper bound 𝑆 𝑁 . Next, the merged entities are mapped into a multimodal feature space compris- ing titles, descriptions, graph neighbours, and numerical attributes. The optimal number of clusters 𝐾 ∗ in the adaptive clustering module is au- tomatically selected using a composite scoring function, yielding more precise groupings. Finally, the lightweight knowledge completion mod- ule adopts a two-stage “embedding-based recall, LLM-based filtering” strategy: candidate triples are retrieved via TransE embeddings, then semantically verified and normalised through a large language model. Composite scoring function and adaptive selection of k Industrial corpora usually follow a long-tail distribution. If the Sil- houette coefficient is isolated, the algorithm tends to favour few clusters, losing fine-grained distinctions; conversely, relying only on the Davies– Bouldin Index (DBI) risks overfitting to local noise. We, therefore, define a composite scoring function that balances both criteria while explicitly discouraging an excessive cluster count: Score( 𝐾 ) = Silhouette( 𝐅 , 𝐾 ) ln ( 𝐾 + 1 ) − 𝛼 DBI( 𝐅 , 𝐾 ) − 𝛽𝐾, (5) where 𝛼 and 𝛽 are non-negative weighting factors. The interval bounds were derived from prior exploratory ex- periments that delineated the sensitivity region of Score( 𝐾 ) . sections.heading: Experiment
sections.text: This section presents a series of controlled experiments to evalu- ate the performance and robustness of the proposed GraphRAG-ASCOC framework and downstream modules. The experiments are structured to address three core tasks: validating synonym merging accuracy, opti- mising adaptive clustering behaviour, and assessing the impact of mul- timodal features. Finally, a human-in-the-loop evaluation is conducted to verify the effectiveness of the lightweight completion module. All experiments share a unified input source and fixed processing pipeline, ensuring comparability under a closed-world setting. To make the role of feature composition explicit, Section 4.3 examines how combining the T/D/G/N affects the adaptive clustering step introduced in Section 3 . The study is performed on the post-consolidation graph, and its out- comes are later used, without changing the completion algorithm, as inputs to the lightweight completion experiment. While the experiments are conducted on structured documents, the framework is equally applicable to unstructured inputs, as GraphRAG operates directly on raw text without relying on predefined structure. 4.1. Dataset The corpus used in this study is drawn from selected sections of the MIL-STD-6016B specification. The original GraphRAG-ASCOC framework first processes raw text to extract entities and subject– predicate–object triples. The downstream modules (i.e., synonym merg- ing, adaptive clustering, and lightweight completion) then iteratively generate and update intermediate artefacts. These include the de- duplicated entity list, the cleaned triple set, and multimodal feature matrices. All subsequent experiments reuse these artefacts without ad- ditional external data, guaranteeing a consistent data source and a fully closed workflow. 4.2. Experiment 1: validation of synonym-merging The corpus parsed from MIL-STD-6016B Chapter 4 contains 1230 dis- tinct entity titles and 1838 RDF triples. Two military communications experts double-annotated a stratified sample of 300 title pairs as “syn- onym” or “non-synonym”, with a Cohen’s 𝑘𝑎𝑝𝑝𝑎 of 0.942 ( Warrens , 2015 ); a third expert resolved disagreements to obtain the gold set 𝑃 . Three runs are evaluated. A0 : no merging; A1 : Levenshtein similarity ≥ 0 . 85 ( Zhang et al. , 2017 ); A2 : the proposed FAISS+MNN scheme, where Sentence-BERT embeddings are reduced to 64 dimensions (SVD) and indexed by FAISS. We report (i) Compression Rate (CR, the fraction of titles that re- main), (ii) Relation Retention (RR, the fraction of triples that survive, self-loops removed), and (iii) Precision, Recall, and 𝐹 1 on 𝑃 . McNemar’s test ( 𝛼 = 0 . 05 ) is used for significance. As shown in Table 2 , our proposed FAISS+MNN approach (A2) reduces the title vocabulary to 83.6 % of its original size, removing more redundancy than the character-based baseline A1, yet still re- tains 97.39 % of the triples–slightly above A1’s 96.95 %. Experiment 4: expert validation of the TLC module This experiment evaluates the effectiveness and cost-efficiency of the proposed TLC framework by performing expert validation over candidate triples generated under various strategies. We use a sin- gle OWL ontology and construct ten different random seeds. Two can- didate sets are generated for each seed: the first by randomly sampling 50 entity pairs and the second by extracting the top 50 scoring pairs according to a TransE model trained on the known triples. This yielded 20 datasets in total. Each candidate set is processed in one of four settings. The first uses manually curated triples written by two domain experts and merged af- ter deduplication. The second involves direct expert judgment over can- didates without any LLM assistance. The remaining two settings incorpo- rate large language models (LLMs) to filter or validate the candidates. We include four popular LLMs in the comparison: GPT-4o, DeepSeek- Chat, Grok-1.5, and LLaMA-70B. The LLM is queried using a structured prompt for each candidate triple, and only those judged as True are re- tained. As a result, the number of triples passed to expert review ( Pred- Size ) varies by model and strategy. Two domain experts independently assess the remaining triples. A triple is considered a true positive (TP) when both experts judge it cor- rect, and as a false positive (FP) when both agree it is incorrect. All disagreements are discarded. Table 3 reports the average results across 10 seeds. Metrics include precision, recall, F1 score, and error rate. Random-only yielded the lowest precision (0.18), with over 80 % of triples being rejected. TransE-only improves this to 0.58 but still incurs a high false-positive rate. LLM filtering doubles the precision of random candidates, albeit at the Cost of increased inference time and API usage. Notably, TransE + GPT-4o achieves the highest quality overall, with a precision of 0.94 and an F1 score of 0.45. At the same Time, TransE + DeepSeek-Chat provides the most cost-effective option–achieving near- optimal precision (0.92) with an average cost of only $0.005 and a run- time of 20 s per dataset. Manual completion remains the gold standard in quality, but its time cost is significantly higher. These results confirm that the proposed TLC module is capable of de- livering high-confidence ontology augmentation at minimal cost, espe- cially when integrated with modern LLMs in a filtered-inference setup. We further note that completion quality is sensitive to the choice of LLM, underscoring the need to balance model capability and efficiency. 4.6. sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Our study is the first to pair a two-stage embedding recall with LLM validation for ontology completion. We introduce a three-stage, closed- loop pipeline that (i) removes lexical redundancy via MNN–FAISS syn- onym merging, (ii) produces coherent clusters with multimodal features and an adaptive scoring function, and (iii) ranks candidate triples with TransE before LLM filtering. On MIL-STD-6016B, the pipeline cuts the title vocabulary to 83.6 % while keeping 97.4 % of triples, raises the Sil- houette, Davies–Bouldin and Calinski–Harabasz scores, and lifts com- pletion precision to 0.94 with an F1 of 0.45–results stable across ten random seeds. Expert evaluations further show that our approach out- performs both the strengthened GraphRAG-KM baseline and pure LLM pipelines. Module-wise runtime and token-cost profiling likewise sub- stantiates its lightweight resource footprint. The workflow is label-free, incrementally updateable and supplies high-quality OWL ontologies to downstream expert system reasoning and digital twin simulation. Several limitations remain. Experiment 4 lacked an external bench- mark, and synonym merging relied on a manually annotated gold set. Future work will release shared corpora and evaluation protocols, ex- tend the framework to multilingual standards, and test lightweight prompting to cut validation latency without sacrificing precision.

claims.text: Our study is the first to pair a two-stage embedding recall with LLM validation for ontology completion. We introduce a three-stage, closed-loop pipeline that removes lexical redundancy, produces coherent clusters, and ranks candidate triples with TransE before LLM filtering.

The pipeline cuts the title vocabulary to 83.6% while keeping 97.4% of triples, raises the Silhouette, Davies-Bouldin and Calinski-Harabasz scores, and lifts completion precision to 0.94 with an F1 of 0.45.
Expert evaluations show that our approach outperforms both the strengthened GraphRAG-KM baseline and pure LLM pipelines.
Several limitations remain, including the lack of an external benchmark in Experiment 4 and the reliance on a manually annotated gold set for synonym merging.
